(255.69/255.33 tok/s), decode853.92/853.06 ms. All four generated texts
match. Combined extended sorting plus adaptive N8 reduces mean prefill
time by49.91% (1.996× throughput) for this365-token prompt, while decode
is essentially unchanged. This is one sequential process pair, not yet an
independent repetition. `MOLLM_CUDA_NVFP4_MMA_PREFILL_SORT=1` now isolates
the extended4096-route sorting without N8; default remains off. Its model
run is pending at `build_cuda/qwen38-native-mma-sort-only-prefill-long.log`.

The sort-only native run completed: prefill744.89/743.41 ms
(490.00/490.98 tok/s), decode844.63/843.78 ms. All six texts (control,
sort-only, adaptive-N8) match. Extended sorting accounts for most of the
combined gain: 1.920× native prefill throughput versus original control;
adaptive N8 adds another1.040× versus sort-only on this prompt. These
single sequential pairs need independent repetition before default promotion.

`MOLLM_CUDA_NVFP4_PREFILL_SORT=1` now enables the same extended sorting
for either SIMT or native MMA, without requiring calibration or a new
package. The earlier MMA-prefixed name remains an alias; the generic name
takes precedence, including explicit0. All CUDA regressions pass with the
generic flag. Original uncalibrated-package SIMT validation is running at
`build_cuda/qwen38-simt-sort-only-prefill-long-old-package.log`.

Authoritative loader evidence reveals an important graph difference: the
original package has `prefill_seq=32`, while the calibrated conversion has
`prefill_seq=256`. The old-package flag test completed at130.29/129.82 tok/s
(2801.42/2811.52 ms), but no extended-sort calls were reported: 32-token
chunks never reach the128-token activation gate. It proves compatibility,
NOT old-package acceleration. The generic sort does not need calibration
tables or change weight layout, but exploiting the larger batches requires
a package with a larger prefill graph. A same-256-graph SIMT sort test is
now running at `build_cuda/qwen38-simt-sort-only-prefill-long.log`; this
keeps activation calibration unused and isolates the SIMT sort capability.

The 256-graph SIMT sort run completed with prefill1905.98/1913.07 ms
(191.50/190.79 tok/s), decode831.46/828.87 ms, and144 extended-sort calls.
This confirms the generic path actually activates without MMA/calibration.
The same-graph same-SIMT no-sort control is now running at
`build_cuda/qwen38-simt-sort-only-prefill-long-control.log`. Do not use the
32-graph result to attribute a sort-only gain, or the native-MMA result to
attribute an arithmetic-identical speedup.

The same-graph SIMT no-sort control completed: prefill2136.10/2139.46 ms
(170.87/170.60 tok/s), decode836.37/835.23 ms. All four generated texts
match. Extended sorting improves SIMT throughput by11.95% on this prompt
(10.67% less prefill time), without activation FP4 quantization or MMA.
An independent four-repeat sorted SIMT process is pending at
`build_cuda/qwen38-simt-sort-only-prefill-long-repeat4.log` before any
SM121-only default promotion. Do not generalize this to other GPU models
or to the32-token original prefill graph.

The independent sorted SIMT process completed four times:
1921.25/1919.10/1920.10/1915.40 ms (189.98–190.56 tok/s). All six texts
from this run plus the two unsorted-control repeats match. Relative to the
control mean, throughput improves11.41%, reproducing the earlier11.95%.
Extended4096-route sorting is now default only on SM121, with device
capability cached at backend construction. Generic/legacy explicit1 forces
it, explicit0 restores the2048-route policy (when batched MMA is disabled);
generic overrides the legacy alias. Other architectures remain unchanged,
as do decode, short batches and the original32-token graph. No arithmetic
precision or weight-layout change is introduced by this default.

`mollm_chat`, `mollm_bench` and CUDA tests were rebuilt; CUDA regressions
pass after promotion. A fresh model test with both sort environment names
explicitly removed completed at
`build_cuda/qwen38-simt-default-sort-prefill-long.log`: prefill1908.87/1905.22 ms,
decode831.20/831.63 ms and144 extended-sort calls. Both generated texts match
the unsorted control, confirming default activation and about12.1% higher
prefill throughput. Native MMA and adaptive-N8 remain opt-in.

The sorting launcher now forwards the caller's CUDA stream instead of using
the implicit default stream. A regression captures sorting on a nonblocking
stream and replays twice, checking stable duplicate-key ordering and paired
gate/down route mapping against a CPU reference at1/2048/2560/4096 routes.
The complete CUDA backend test passes; bench/chat binaries were rebuilt.

This page collects the CPU, CUDA and Metal benchmark results used by the README.

### Resident allocator repeated comparison (2026-10-05)

Four serial fresh processes in host/device/device/host order, with dense
row-major sidecars explicitly disabled, warmup 1 and repeat 4, produced:

| Expert arena | Decode tok/s, four generations |
| --- | --- |
| Host huge-page arena | 37.84 / 37.66 / 37.70 / 37.61 |
| CUDA device arena | 37.82 / 37.77 / 37.99 / 37.77 |
| CUDA device arena | 37.78 / 37.75 / 37.76 / 37.73 |
| Host huge-page arena | 37.53 / 37.52 / 37.71 / 37.69 |

Eight-generation medians are 37.675 versus 37.770 tok/s, only +0.25%
for CUDA allocation. Host prefill spans 122.37–123.61 tok/s versus
117.15–118.40 for device allocation. This does not justify enabling the
device arena by default. All sixteen generated-text/EOS report blocks
match the fixed reference exactly; each process also checks repeated greedy
token IDs internally. Process peak RSS is about 70,082 MiB versus 4,939 MiB,
but CUDA driver allocations are not represented by that RSS difference:
both modes retain the same 63.633 GiB expert payload on this unified-memory
machine. No additional memory telemetry was collected for these runs.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-arena-repeat-{1-1,2-cuda-device,3-cuda-device,4-1}.log`.

The standalone native MMA probe now also accepts a fixed activation global
dequantization scale while recomputing each 16-element block's E4M3 scale.
This distinction matters: NVIDIA ModelOpt's [NVFP4 backend](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer/blob/main/modelopt/torch/quantization/backends/nvfp4_gemm.py)
uses calibrated input amax when available and passes its reciprocal global
multiplier to the activation quantizer. Fixed global scaling does not mean
fixed per-block activation scales. The probe's scale argument instead uses
dequantization units, not that reciprocal multiplier.

Twelve new synthetic checks cover two resident layouts, zero activations,
ragged 19-row tiles, and global scales 0.0013892765, 0.0031854538 and 0.00001.
Maximum normalized MMA error against independently decoded W4/A4 double
accumulation is 1.11e-6. The deliberately tiny scale saturates and yields
96% activation-induced output relative L2 error despite correct MMA, making
explicit why kernel parity alone cannot validate model quality. This is not
checkpoint quantizer parity or a model accuracy result; activation conversion
still runs on the CPU outside timed kernel sections. Log:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-fixed-global-probe.log`.

The probe now feeds MMA with GPU-produced activations. A block-owned CUDA
quantizer computes each 16-value maximum, converts its E4M3 scale and packs
E2M1 pairs using round-to-nearest division. All packed activation bytes and
scale bytes match the separate CPU implementation for the existing dynamic
global diagnostics and twelve fixed-global cases; all native layout/split
checks still pass. This is probe parity, not parity with an external
checkpoint quantizer. GPU quantization alone takes 3.83–4.11 us in this run.
For the selected packed eight-warp kernels (eight K parts for gate/up and
one for down), quantization plus MMA takes 118.73–119.19 us for N1280/K2560
and 65.25–72.36 us for N2560/K640 across the two input layouts. Ratios
against SIMT are 0.973–0.976 and 0.925–0.930 respectively: this implementation
does not yet accelerate decode. These are rotating 128-MiB-or-larger synthetic
weight sets, not a model-sized throughput measurement. No production default
or checkpoint conversion changed. Log:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-gpu-activation-combined.log`.

An MMA-native L2-prefetch specialization reads ahead one split-K iteration
over the four contiguous register planes of each packed weight tile. It
changes no arithmetic and passes the independently decoded reference check.
Three fresh probe processes show gate/up quantization-plus-MMA prefetch
ratios of 0.964–1.050 and down ratios of 1.000–1.056 across the two original
layouts. Absolute prefetched timings are 118.80–122.70 us and 64.84–65.13 us.
The gate/up effect is inconsistent, and this does not establish superiority
to SIMT or an end-to-end model improvement. The specialization is used only
by the standalone diagnostic; production code is unchanged. Logs:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-prefetch-{1,2,3}.log`.

A shared-memory fused activation-quantization/MMA specialization now avoids
the standalone activation launch and global packed-activation intermediate.
The first version redundantly quantized the whole input for each split-K
CTA: gate/up timings were 118.00–126.08 us and down 61.67–62.15 us. The
revised version quantizes only the 64-element K tiles owned by that CTA.
Three processes give gate/up 114.66–118.27 us and down 61.72–62.09 us.
Ratios against SIMT span 0.976–1.066 and 0.973–1.038; these small synthetic
effects do not yet establish a model speedup. This remains diagnostic-only.

Fused parity covers both original resident layouts, K64/128/640/2560,
ragged rows 3/7/19, zero and varied activations, fixed-global saturation
cases, one/two/four/eight warps and one/two/four/eight K splits. The CTA
barrier precedes ragged-warp return; unowned shared K tiles are never read.
All checks pass the decoded W4/A4 double reference with normalized maximum
error tolerance 2e-5. This does not validate checkpoint activation metadata
or model accuracy. Logs: `build_cuda/nvfp4-fused-quantization-{1,2,3}.log`,
`build_cuda/nvfp4-fused-split-quantization-{1,2,3}.log`, and
`build_cuda/nvfp4-fused-ragged-validation.log`.

The fused kernel was also measured with one complete 68,325,212,160-byte
synthetic expert payload (48 layers, 512 experts, rotating groups of ten).
Host allocation gives gate/up 115.67–116.00 us versus SIMT 117.27–118.06 us,
and down 61.81–61.96 versus 61.25–61.67 us. CUDA allocation gives gate/up
89.36–89.51 versus 97.42–98.22 us and down 48.30–48.48 versus 58.43–58.69 us.
All three repetitions and analytic finite-output checks pass in each mode.

A subsequent CUDA run adds the crucial packed-but-unfused control: gate/up
packed native MMA is 89.14–89.31 us versus fused 89.51–89.61; down's first
two repetitions are 48.35–48.45 versus fused 48.59–48.78 us. Thus the
large-pool gain comes principally from packed weight addressing with CUDA
allocation, not from fused quantization itself. This control's unfused
timing excludes activation quantization. Constant synthetic weight/scales
represent identical matrices in both layouts, enabling this comparison with
one payload; it does not validate repacking real model weights. Production
integration still requires checkpoint scaling metadata, single-copy native
resident preparation and end-to-end accuracy/performance validation.
Logs: `build_cuda/nvfp4-large-fused-{host,device}.log` and
`build_cuda/nvfp4-large-fused-packed-control.log`.

The streamed Qwen4/Qwen3.8 converter now preserves expert activation
calibration as separate FP32 metadata weights:
`*_mlp_experts_gate_up_input_scales` has shape [experts, 2] (gate then up),
and `*_mlp_experts_down_input_scales` has shape [experts, 1]. Original scalar
bytes/units are retained, with no reciprocal conversion or assumption that
gate and up share a global scale. Complete absence remains compatible with
uncalibrated older inputs; partial metadata fails conversion. Non-F32,
non-scalar, nonpositive, nonfinite and truncated scales are rejected.

Read-only validation of the original checkpoint covers all 48 layers and
512 experts: 73,728 finite positive activation scalars, totaling 294,912
payload bytes. The existing converted model has not been rewritten and the
runtime does not yet consume this metadata. Unit checks verify expert-major
projection order, distinct gate/up bytes, invalid shapes/names/values and
unchanged expert pair-packed payload. This closes a conversion prerequisite,
not an end-to-end performance or checkpoint-quantizer parity gate.

`launch_repack_nvfp4_mma` is now an allocation-free, stream-aware CUDA
preparation primitive. It converts either row-major or four-row pair-packed
E2M1 weights plus row-major E4M3 block scales into the native register-plane
and scale-selector layout, zero-padding incomplete 16-row tiles. Row-global
scales are untouched. Source and destination must not overlap, and source
staging must outlive stream completion. The interface permits bounded
projection-sized staging into one final resident arena; it is not yet wired
into the resident provider, so no model-sized storage-policy change is claimed.

The probe independently constructs the CPU reference, overwrites the prepared
layout through this launcher, and checks all weight/scale bytes before MMA.
Coverage includes both layouts, ragged rows 3/7/19, K64/128/640/2560,
varied weights/scales and full projection shapes. Separate CUDA-allocated
destinations are checked on the small cases; invalid K, zero rows and
unaligned target weights are rejected. Existing native/fused MMA checks
pass using the GPU-repacked payload. Log:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-gpu-repack-validation.log`.

The resident provider can now prepare native MMA layout with explicit
`MOLLM_RESIDENT_NVFP4_MMA_LAYOUT=1` plus
`MOLLM_RESIDENT_EXPERT_ARENA=cuda-device`. It requires NVFP4, rows divisible
by 16, K divisible by 64 and coherent pageable host memory with host page
tables. Workers repack their bounded CPU staging directly into the final
CUDA allocation, then copy unchanged row globals and synchronize before
publishing Ready. Runtime-only layout markers distinguish raw whole-layer
views; ordinary CPU borrows inverse-repack temporary projection-sized host
copies, preserving all original bytes. The provider fixture verifies layout
markers, exact CPU fallback, one-payload accounting and clearing capabilities.

The production CUDA SIMT reader also understands this layout with the same
FP32 activation/FMA/reduction arithmetic. This is not yet native FP4 MMA
inference and does not consume activation calibration. Before compile-time
reader specialization, two warm generations in native layout produced
35.28/35.25 decode and 106.37/106.43 prefill tok/s, versus old-layout control
36.91/37.25 and 111.25/110.17. All four complete 174-token text/EOS reports
match the fixed reference. The new layout is therefore not a recommended
SIMT configuration. Readers are now separate compile-time specializations
to avoid native indexing in the default path; cache and CUDA backend unit
tests pass. Post-specialization warmup-1/repeat-2 model comparisons give
native-layout SIMT decode 34.75/34.75 and prefill 111.15/111.21 tok/s versus
old-layout decode 37.47/37.63 and prefill 119.08/119.47. Both processes finish
successfully and all four full text/EOS blocks match the reference. This
confirms the native-prepared SIMT path is correct on the fixed generation,
but slower and still disabled by default. Logs also include
`build_cuda/qwen38-native-layout-specialized-{1,0}.log`.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-native-layout-{simt,control}.log`,
`build_cuda/native-layout-{provider,backend}-specialized-tests.log`.

Calibration export now has graph constant references as well as streamed
entries: the package writer collects only graph-referenced weights, so the
earlier streamed-only addition did not itself guarantee inclusion. Metadata
constants are unused by MoE arithmetic and emitted only for checkpoints with
calibration. The per-projection storage metadata now resolves their exact
weight/data offsets, byte counts and one/two scales per expert. Tests write
and reread a complete tiny `.mollm` package and verify calibrated bytes at
those resolved offsets; graph tests check both references per layer and
unchanged MoE operator count. Missing or malformed calibration entries fail
packaging. The existing full model package remains unchanged.

Runtime package loading now reads these small FP32 tables into expert-source
metadata, preserving expert-major gate/up order and original scale units.
It checks the package weight map, XMAP type/shape/flags and bounded offsets,
then rejects incomplete, nonpositive or nonfinite calibration. Sources from
older packages explicitly retain empty calibration; no dynamic-amax policy is
silently substituted. These values are not yet consumed by a production MMA
kernel, so this change does not establish a new throughput or quality result.
`test_nvfp4_calibration_package` loads a complete tiny dense package with unused
NVFP4 expert/calibration constants, rejects seven corrupted variants (zero,
negative, infinity, NaN, wrong type/shape, out-of-bounds offset), and successfully
reloads and infers afterward. It passes in CUDA and CPU-only builds; provider
tests also check distinct gate/up values and uncalibrated-source compatibility.
The fixture tests loading, not real-model NVFP4 tensor-core numerical quality.

An experimental runtime MMA path is now wired behind
`MOLLM_CUDA_NVFP4_MMA=1`, requiring `MOLLM_RESIDENT_EXPERT_ARENA=cuda-device`
and `MOLLM_RESIDENT_NVFP4_MMA_LAYOUT=1`. It uses the single-copy native
resident payload and per-expert checkpoint globals. Gate and up select their
own global at the output-row boundary; each CTA quantizes its input into shared
FP4/E4M3 blocks before native m16n8k64 MMA. Calibration is required rather than
substituted from activation amax. The current kernel supports K up to 2560,
64-aligned split rows and 16-aligned output rows on SM120/121.
For this mode only, route weights are applied to down outputs, not to its
inputs: fixed-global activation quantization cannot commute with route
weighting. Default SIMT arithmetic and activation ordering remain unchanged.
The standalone probe checks the reusable runtime kernel against independent
CPU-double decoded quantized references, including distinct expert/gate/up
globals, output-side weighting and partial CTAs. All cases pass the 2e-5
normalized-error gate; the CUDA backend regression also passes. Log:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-runtime-mma-validation.log`. Real-model quality and throughput
remain unvalidated; this mode is not enabled by default.

The complete calibrated model package was subsequently converted locally
(123,744,966,724 bytes, 96 calibration tables totaling 294,912 payload bytes).
SIMT on this package gives 37.30/37.29 tok/s decode and 117.78/118.32 prefill;
both 174-token output/EOS blocks match the old-package reference exactly.
Initial native MMA gives 37.73/37.73 decode and 167.11/167.21 prefill, with a
stable but different 167-token generation and correct arithmetic answer.
Different generation lengths prevent a strict decode speedup claim.
Teacher-forced decode on the self-authored bilingual sanity fixture has 357
tokens/356 targets: SIMT CE/PPL=2.348500/10.469850 at 35.65 tok/s, initial MMA
2.296945/9.943756 at 35.81 tok/s. This is a small sanity check, not a standard
or comprehensive quality benchmark. Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-calibrated-*`.

An eight-part gate/up split-K runtime experiment passes independent numerical
checks at parts 1/2/4/8, but real-model decode stays 37.76/37.75 tok/s and
prefill regresses to 159.65/159.69. Therefore split-K is not the runtime
default; `MOLLM_CUDA_NVFP4_MMA_GATE_PARTS=2|4|8` retains diagnostic access.
Logs: `build_cuda/nvfp4-runtime-splitk-validation.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-native-mma-splitk.log`. The requested end-to-end decode
optimization remains unfinished.

Fresh Nsight Systems node-level capture of the initial native-MMA mode isolates
the final 166 decode tokens by LM-head boundaries, excluding loading, repacking,
warmup and prefill. The instrumented window is 4502.407 ms; summed kernel time
is 4260.136 ms (94.6% of that window). Kernel-time shares are native expert MMA
27.53%, row-parallel W4 22.41%, wide W4 22.19%, pair-row W4 5.65%, Q8 LM head
10.01%, GDN 3.35%, group RMS norm 2.55%, routing 2.09%. Thus dense W4 accounts
for 50.25% of GPU kernel time, and CPU/GPU gaps are not the dominant bottleneck
in this capture. Do not report profiler-instrumented speed as benchmark speed.
The wide N16480/K2560 path averages 123.07 us; the N2560 row-parallel family
averages 52.85 us. Existing swizzle experiments were already negative end-to-end,
so this does not justify repeating that change. Next investigation should focus
on dense projection execution and memory throughput rather than expert split-K.
Report: `build_cuda/qwen38-native-mma-decode-profile.nsys-rep`; filtered analysis
is reproducible with `tools/analyze_cuda_decode_profile.py <export.sqlite>
--decode-tokens 166`. This tool requires a verified one-LM-head-per-token trace.
The root profiling tool is Nsight 2025.6.3; the user's 2025.3.2 tool cannot read
its newer reports, so export/stats must use the matching version.

A read-only audit of all 628 dense W4G32 weights finds 114,339,840 FP32
scale values, only 1,808 unique bit patterns. Every value can be encoded as
a 16-bit BF16 maximum and reconstructed by round-to-nearest FP32 division by
7 with identical bits. This is not ordinary FP16 rounding of the scale.
Keeping nibbles unchanged and replacing eight FP32 scales per BG32 block with
eight 16-bit codes would reduce 2,286,796,800 payload bytes to 2,058,117,120
(228,679,680 bytes saved, 10%). `tools/audit_q4_scale_encoding.py` reproduces
this check without changing the package. This property has only been verified
for this package; any implementation must validate it and retain a general
fallback. A compact runtime kernel has not yet been implemented or benchmarked,
and additional scale-decoding work may offset the saved memory traffic.

### Experimental register-resident CUDA routing (2026-10-05)

`MOLLM_CUDA_REGISTER_ROUTES=1` keeps per-lane top-k candidates at static
register indices instead of a dynamically indexed local array. It remains
disabled by default. SM121 resource inspection reports 128 bytes of thread
stack for the original path and zero for both register specializations
(16 candidates through 512 experts; 32 through 1024).

The full 174-token greedy generation matches the existing reference exactly.
Node traces report mean route-kernel duration 8.30 us versus 12.25 us in the
earlier control trace; these are separate traces, not clock-controlled runs.
Four fresh, serial warmup-1 model runs with the current W4 prefetch default,
host resident arena and PLE offload give:

| Routing | Decode tok/s | Prefill tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Original | 37.54 | 124.04 |
| Registers | 37.57 | 122.38 |
| Original | 37.53 | 123.47 |
| Registers | 37.96 | 121.20 |

All four outputs match exactly. The paired decode gains are only 0.08% and
1.15%; this is insufficient evidence for a reliable whole-model gain or a
default switch. Logs are `build_cuda/qwen38-register-routes-warm-*.log`;
the full node trace is `build_cuda/qwen38-register-routes-nodes.nsys-rep`.
Dedicated CTest coverage exercises the opt-in path, including 511/512/513
expert specialization boundaries, three score functions and equal-score ties.

### W8 LM-head L2-prefetch diagnostic (2026-10-05)

`bench_cuda_projections --q8` tests the real 248320-by-2560 output-head
shape with varied int8 weights, per-channel scales and FP32 activations.
Weight size is 635699200 bytes, larger than the cache; each candidate keeps
the original FMA order and warp reduction. All output rows compare bit-exact
against the no-prefetch kernel. Three serial runs give 2487–2497 us for the
control and 2503–2542 us for prefetch distances 1/2/4 warp iterations.
No variant wins (speedup 0.982–0.996). The control's weight-only effective
throughput is about 255 GB/s; this is not a hardware-counter measurement.
The production selector remains unchanged. Diagnostic logs are
`build_cuda/q8-prefetch-{1,2,3}.log`; the standalone diagnostic also compares
against the production launcher in `q8-prefetch-production-control.log`.

### Narrow W4 L2-prefetch experiment (2026-10-05)

The diagnostic keeps the 256-thread per-row accumulation and reduction
unchanged, prefetching future packed bytes and group scales. At 2560-by-6144,
distance 4 gives microbenchmark speedups 1.064/1.055/1.073 in three fresh
serial runs; distances 1/2 regress. At 320-by-10240, distance 4 gives
0.904/0.978/1.046 and is not selected. Every rotating weight set compares
bit-exact. Logs: `build_cuda/q4-narrow-prefetch-{2560,320}-{1,2,3}.log`.

`MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_NARROW_PREFETCH=1` experimentally selects distance 4 only for
the aligned 2560-by-6144 GEMV; it remains disabled by default. Four serial
warmup-1 full model runs (off/on/off/on) produce decode rates
37.94/37.47/36.94/37.93 tok/s and prefill rates
121.29/123.76/123.71/123.34 tok/s. All four 174-token greedy outputs match
the reference exactly. Paired decode changes -1.24%/+2.68% are inconclusive;
these are not frequency-locked runs. No reliable whole-model improvement
is claimed. Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-q4-narrow-warm-*.log`.
The dedicated opt-in CTest and normal CUDA backend test exercise the actual
2560-by-6144 shape, comparing all rows bit-exact to the original kernel.

### Eight-row and split-K narrow W4 diagnostics (2026-10-05)

Directly reusing the existing 16-lane-per-row kernel for eight output rows
per CTA does not improve the narrow shapes. Three rotating-weight runs at
2560-by-6144 give 64.6–68.5 us uncached and 71.2–71.8 us with cached
activations versus 59.4–61.0 us controls. At 320-by-10240, candidates take
40.0–46.2 us versus mostly 17.9–18.0 us controls.

A diagnostic split-K variant assigns 2/4/8 independent 16-lane groups to
each of the eight rows, combining their partial results in shared memory.
At 2560-by-6144 the best stable candidate is approximately 63.4 us (split 8),
still slower than ordinary controls around 56.7–60.7 us. At 320-by-10240,
split 8 ranges 17.6–21.2 us, without a repeatable gain against approximately
18 us controls. Isolated outlier controls at 86.3 and 26.3 us must not be
interpreted as candidate wins.

These paths change the FP32 reduction order; they are not bit-exact. All
tested rotating sets remain finite and pass the synthetic comparison
threshold; maximum absolute difference from the original is 5.35e-5 for
pair-row and 3.06e-5 for split-K. This is not model-level quality validation.
No production selector invokes either diagnostic, so there is no full-model
speedup or quality claim. Normal CUDA regressions also cover these launchers
on the actual 2560-by-6144 shape with a 1e-3 absolute comparison tolerance.
Logs: `build_cuda/q4-pair-narrow-{2560,320}-{1,2,3}.log` and
`build_cuda/q4-split-pair-{2560,320}-{1,2,3}.log`.

### Experimental row-contiguous narrow W4 layout (2026-10-05)

`MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_ROW_MAJOR=1` adds GPU-only row-contiguous sidecars for
2560-by-6144 and 320-by-10240 weights. Each group stores its FP32 scale and
16 biased packed bytes (20 bytes total). The GEMV retains the original
256-thread per-row accumulation and reduction order. Other shapes, unaligned
activation pointers and multi-row prefill keep the original path; original
packed device weights remain available for prefill. Default is disabled.
The package, CPU buffers and original NFS checkpoint are unchanged.

Three rotating-weight microbenchmarks compare every set bit-exact:
2560-by-6144 speedups 1.194/1.093/1.160, and 320-by-10240
1.263/1.239/1.197. Four fresh serial warmup-1 model runs (off/on/off/on)
give decode 37.45/38.79/37.55/37.77 tok/s and prefill
123.85/122.17/123.17/123.15 tok/s. Both paired decode differences are
positive (+3.58%/+0.59%), but the small sample and unlocked clocks do not
establish a stable whole-model gain. All four 174-token outputs match the
reference exactly. Logs: `build_cuda/q4-row-major-{2560,320}-{1,2,3}.log`
and `build_cuda/qwen38-q4-row-major-warm-*.log`.

The rebuilt 32-token node trace matches the earlier 32-token output exactly
and confirms execution of the row-contiguous kernels (1440 N2560 calls at
48.03 us, 2910 N320 calls at 13.00 us after excluding prefill and the first
decode). It reports 145 sidecars totaling 670515200 bytes (639.45 MiB).
This is additional CUDA-allocated RAM, despite essentially unchanged process
RSS; it is not a memory-saving layout. Steady decode has the same 57482
kernel count as the control, so repacking is not repeated during decode.
Trace: `build_cuda/qwen38-q4-row-major-nodes.nsys-rep`.
Dedicated CTest coverage checks GPU repacking and bit-exact GEMV against
the original, and backend dispatch after clearing the CPU packed source.

The additional 640-by-2560 shape has three microbenchmark speedups
1.148/1.144/1.131, all rotating sets bit-exact. In contrast, 512-by-2560
gives 0.999/0.923/1.000 and 4-by-2560 gives approximately 1.001–1.004;
neither is selected. Logs: `build_cuda/q4-row-major-extra-{640,512,4}-{1,2,3}.log`.

`MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_ROW_MAJOR=2` retains level 1's two shapes and additionally
selects 640-by-2560. Level 1's behavior is unchanged; default remains off.
Four fresh serial warmup-1 model runs (off/2/off/2) give decode
37.93/38.58/38.11/38.51 tok/s and prefill
123.16/123.48/123.47/121.30 tok/s. Both paired decode gains are positive
(+1.71%/+1.05%), but there is no matched level-1 comparison in this batch,
so it does not establish a benefit of level 2 over level 1. All four
174-token outputs match the reference exactly. Sidecars total 241 weights,
768819200 bytes (733.20 MiB), including an additional 93.75 MiB over level 1.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-q4-row-major-extended-*.log`. Dedicated level-2
CTest coverage exercises all three selected shapes, including GPU repacking,
bit-exact GEMV and backend dispatch after clearing the CPU source.

### Repeated generation and level-1/2 comparison (2026-10-05)

`mollm_bench --repeat N` now performs N separately timed generations after
one load and the requested warmups (default N=1, accepted range 1..10000).
Each generation resets its context and per-run profiling/cache counters;
weights and the resident expert cache remain loaded. `benchmark_run=N`
delimits repeated reports. Load time and process peak RSS are shared values,
not per-generation measurements. With temperature zero, repeated token IDs,
text and EOS must agree or the benchmark fails. Reports are flushed before
backend teardown to prevent stderr diagnostics splitting generated text in
merged logs; the initial unflushed diagnostic log is not an output reference.

Four fresh processes in level order 1/2/2/1, each with warmup 1 and repeat 4,
produce the following decode rates (tok/s):

| Layout level | Four successive timed generations |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 38.54, 38.50, 38.38, 38.51 |
| 2 | 38.02, 37.99, 37.93, 37.94 |
| 2 | 37.91, 37.90, 37.88, 37.87 |
| 1 | 37.41, 37.40, 37.46, 37.47 |

The eight-run medians are 37.925 and 37.920 respectively. The first/last
level-1 batches differ substantially, so elapsed-time drift remains a
confounder despite stable within-process repeats. This batch establishes no
whole-model benefit of level 2 over level 1; defaults remain unchanged.
All 16 full 174-token generated texts match the earlier reference exactly,
in addition to the benchmark's per-process token/EOS checks. Logs:
`build_cuda/qwen38-layout-repeat-flushed-{1-1,2-2,3-2,4-1}.log`.
`test_bench_repeat_args` checks defaults, bounds, malformed values and a
missing value. The existing single-run KV format gains no repeat marker.

### Read-only GPU-clock sampling and layout off/1 comparison (2026-10-05)

Four fresh processes in order off/1/1/off, warmup 1 and repeat 4, were
accompanied by 500-ms `nvidia-smi` samples. No clock or power settings were
changed. Decode rates (tok/s):

| Layout | Four successive timed generations |
| --- | --- |
| Off | 37.15, 37.09, 37.18, 37.18 |
| 1 | 38.02, 37.97, 37.98, 37.96 |
| 1 | 35.62, 35.62, 35.80, 35.59 |
| Off | 37.29, 37.27, 37.28, 37.38 |

All 16 generated texts match the full 174-token reference exactly. The
large between-process variation of the enabled layout is inconsistent with
a reliable gain; its median is 36.880 versus 37.225 off. Therefore the
earlier positive pairs remain insufficient to enable the layout by default.

Filtering telemetry to GPU utilization >=90% gives 48/46/49/48 samples;
all report software power capping Not Active. Sampled SM clocks range
2463–2476, 2463–2483, 2463–2483 and 2457–2483 MHz respectively. These sparse
samples include warmup/prefill and are not per-kernel clocks; they cannot
fully rule out clock effects, but provide no evidence that a large SM-clock
drop explains the slow enabled process. The historical power-cap counter
observed before the runs does not prove capping during them.

During the fourth process, `smaps_rollup` reports 66723840 KiB AnonHugePages,
consistent with the 63.633-GiB resident expert arena. The third process was
not sampled for huge pages, so its slow result cannot be attributed to a
large-page shortfall. Memory-controller clocks are unavailable through
NVML on this machine. Logs and CSVs: `build_cuda/qwen38-layout-clock-*`.

## CUDA: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next resident + PLE offload

Local validation on 2026-10-05: NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121), 121 GiB host RAM,
CUDA 13.0, driver 580.178.04, Linux 7.0.0-1019-nvidia. The local NVMe package
contains native NVFP4 experts, W4G32 dense weights and a W8 per-channel LM head.
Raw checkpoint files may remain on NFS; these runs read the converted package
from local ext4 storage.

Both backends use eight CPU threads, context 2048, `--offload-ple`, greedy
sampling, no warmup, and the real prompt shown below (24 input tokens).
CUDA values are medians of three fresh processes; CPU is one fresh-process
comparison, not a controlled five-process benchmark. Clocks were not pinned.
The original CUDA row used a plain `121` target; the optimized row uses `121a`.

| Backend | Prefill tok/s | Decode tok/s | TTFT | Peak process RSS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CPU resident + PLE offload | 34.92 | 15.69 | 687 ms | 68.99 GiB |
| CUDA initial implementation | 37.07 | 22.53 | 647 ms | 68.44 GiB |
| CUDA optimized resident + PLE offload | 56.88 | 29.57 | 422 ms | 68.44 GiB |

Optimized decode samples were 29.57, 29.35 and 29.81 tok/s; prefill samples
were 54.19, 57.23 and 56.88 tok/s. This is +31.2% decode, +53.4% prefill and
-34.8% TTFT against the original medians. All three fresh processes generated
the same 174-token answer, reached EOS, and answered `17 × 23 = 391`.
Process RSS was approximately unchanged, with no second expert-weight allocation.
This remains an intermediate performance result, not a claim that CUDA tuning
is finished.

Initial CUDA decode samples were 22.63, 20.95 and 22.53 tok/s. All three generated the
same 170-token response, reached EOS, and correctly answered `17 × 23 = 391`.
CPU generated 174 tokens, also reaching EOS with the correct answer. Expert
misses and evictions were zero throughout generation in both modes. CUDA
initialization took 38.4–41.1 seconds, including eager expert loading/locking
and dense-weight upload; this is separate from TTFT. Process RSS does not
include all CUDA/driver allocations, so it is not a total unified-memory budget.
An after-load process snapshot reported 67.55 GiB locked and no swap usage.

```bash
cmake -S . -B build_cuda -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DMOLLM_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121a -DMOLLM_BUILD_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build_cuda -j 8 --target mollm_chat mollm_bench
./build_cuda/mollm_bench --package ../qwen38_flash_next_nvfp4.mollm \
  --device cuda --offload-ple --threads 8 --n-ctx 2048 \
  --temperature 0 --max-new-tokens 192 --warmup 0 \
  --prompt '请用一句中文介绍你自己，并计算 17 × 23。'
```

CUDA implements the model's sigmoid-gated DeltaNet, gated residual operators,
scalar broadcasts and NVFP4 expert projections. On GB10, expert kernels read
the provider's existing locked host buffers directly; they do not allocate
another full expert copy. Fully resident providers lend each layer once, keep
its expert leases pinned until backend teardown, and select routes on GPU.
Prefill groups expert jobs to reuse weights in cache; eligible Q4 decode
replays a cached MoE subgraph. Narrow W4 projections parallelize K within each
output row, wide W4 kernels vectorize weight/activation loads, and `121a`
enables hardware FP4 conversions. PLE lookup stays
on CPU; PLE gate/convolution run on GPU. Unsupported devices/layouts retain
the CPU bridge.
See [loading requirements](ssd-offload.md#resident-experts-with-ple-paging).

Regression coverage includes both GDN gate variants, resident PLE loading and
failure recovery, exact same-backend PLE-offload logits, NVFP4 layouts/scales,
MoE BF16 boundaries, GPU routing/tie ordering, prefill grouping, graph replay
after scratch/parameter changes, and lease release on native execution or
cache-miss fallback. PLE convolution tests preserve state across padded
prefill, decode and zero-token forwards. Numerical comparisons reject NaNs.
W4 CUDA is checked against an independently dequantized floating-point package
at the existing strict tolerances, because ARM CPU W4 uses INT8 activations.
CPU and CUDA generation need not be token-identical across those arithmetic paths.

Additional CUDA smoke checks reached EOS with a larger 1024-token output limit:
Chinese-to-English translation (34 prompt tokens, 323 generated tokens,
22.55 decode tok/s), and a 120-token background prompt followed by a summary
and `19 × 27 = 513` (389 generated tokens, 64.76 prefill / 22.51 decode tok/s).
The initial 256-token limits truncated these reasoning-model responses, so
those truncated runs are not counted as completed generation checks.

Local logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-final-{1,2,3}.log`,
`build_i8mm/qwen38-final-cpu.log`, `build_cuda/qwen38-final-tests.log`,
`build_i8mm/qwen38-final-tests.log`, and
`build_cuda/qwen38-final-{translation,long}-complete.log`.
Optimized logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-optimized-{1,2,3}.log`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-optimized-tests.log`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-optimized-operator-tests.log`, and
`build_i8mm/qwen38-optimized-tests.log`. Rotating-weight operator benchmarks
are available in `bench_cuda_projections`; their working set exceeds L2.

Further wide-W4 experiments on 2026-10-05 were rejected, not included in the
optimized throughput above. At N=16480/13312, K=2560, one-group-ahead explicit
loads measured 166.32/132.23 us and two-group batched loads 158.57/125.15 us,
versus approximately 153.72/121.90 us before these experiments. Both passed
CUDA operator parity, but neither justified retaining the additional code.
Increasing the CTA from 128 to 256 threads also regressed these shapes
(159.04/127.55 us). Nsight Compute's cold replay reported 79% long-scoreboard
stall contribution and shared-memory-limited 75% theoretical occupancy;
these counters identify latency to investigate, not achievable model speedup.
Local evidence is in `build_cuda/projections-prefetch*.log`,
`build_cuda/projections-occupancy*.log` and `build_cuda/q4-multicast-root-profile.ncu-rep`.

A bounded FP16 dense-W4 prefill-cache prototype was also rejected and removed.
With the same 136-token prompt and 32 generated tokens, cold prefill was
72.28 tok/s with an 8 GiB budget versus 101.57 without it. With one warmup and
`MOLLM_CUDA_PROFILE=1` on both runs, cache/no-cache prefill was 91.61/121.34
tok/s and decode 20.96/29.47 tok/s. The cache held 628 matrices (7,308,165,120
bytes) and reported 5,652 hits, so absence of reuse did not explain the loss.
These are single-run experimental comparisons, not updated production medians.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-prefill-cache-{long,baseline,warm,warm-baseline}.log`.

The current wide-W4 GEMV reads 32-bit packets with four lanes per row/eight
rows per warp. Two lane-local accumulators and packet shuffles preserve the
previous eight-lane FP32 reduction tree; the ragged K=2560 operator test also
compares all 18,439 rows exactly against that tree. Rotating-weight microbench
N=16480/13312, K=2560 measured 145.64/114.74 us. A first whole-model run
measured 29.76 decode tok/s and produced byte-identical text to the prior
optimized reference. This is not sufficient to claim a whole-model speedup
or replace the three-run medians above. Logs: `build_cuda/projections-oct-exact*`,
`build_cuda/projections-oct-reduction*`, `build_cuda/qwen38-oct-exact-1.log`.
The faster reassociated prototype (`qwen38-oct-projections-{1,2,3}.log`) is not
the retained implementation: it altered generation wording.

NVFP4 instruction-level profiling (`build_cuda/nvfp4-resident-root-profile.ncu-rep`)
reported 92% long-scoreboard stall contribution with nominal full occupancy.
The dominant sampled PCs consume packed weight bytes; FP8 scale conversion
has much fewer samples. Two-row/warp 32-bit packet redistribution retained
the old reduction tree and passed parity but did not improve the rotating
gate projection (121.67 us). Explicit read-only weight/scale loads also did
not establish a gain (119.15 us paired, 122.99 us raw); both experiments were
removed. Evidence: `build_cuda/projections-nvfp4-{packets,ldg}*.log` and
`build_cuda/nvfp4-resident-stalls.log`. Counter replay timing is not a
production latency estimate.

TILE now has a native FP32 CUDA implementation for validated repeat shapes
and strided source views, avoiding the CPU staging bridge. A native-only test
checks sliced/row-strided input with repetitions on all four axes exactly.
The model smoke run (`build_cuda/qwen38-native-tile.log`) reported 174 native
TILE calls and only PLE_LOOKUP fallback, byte-identical reference text and
29.93 decode tok/s. This single run is not a replacement for the medians above.

`MOLLM_CUDA_CAPTURE_AUDIT=1` is an opt-in address/shape/parameter diagnostic,
not a performance mode or proof of capture safety. The 32-token model audit
found stable MATMUL/MoE/GR/GDN signatures across decode calls, while SDPA
signatures change with context; cache metadata contents and private scratch
addresses still require separate handling for whole-graph replay.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-capture-audit.log`.

CUDA scratch and boundary buffers now grow geometrically (minimum 4 KiB,
otherwise less than 2x the requested size), avoiding exact-size reallocations
as context exceeds existing capacity. Allocation failure falls back to freeing
the old scratch and requesting the exact size. A boundary regression checks
exact uploaded data and stable addresses inside capacity buckets;
`MOLLM_CUDA_DISABLE_GEOMETRIC_GROWTH=1` retains exact growth for diagnostic
comparisons. Both modes pass CUDA operator parity. Short prefill can already
leave enough spare score capacity for an entire short decode benchmark, so
this does not establish a speedup there. The smoke run
(`build_cuda/qwen38-geometric-growth.log`) produced identical reference text
at 29.19 decode tok/s; production medians have not been updated.

Experimental decode segment replay is built with
`-DMOLLM_CUDA_DECODE_SEGMENTS=ON` (default OFF), which uses the per-thread
default CUDA stream. `MOLLM_CUDA_DISABLE_DECODE_SEGMENTS=1` disables replay
within the same build for A/B testing. After a warm decode call, GPU work
following PLE lookup is captured between dynamic attention calls; SDPA and
CPU fallback remain ordinary submissions. The LM-head tail flushes the final
segment before reading its result. Tensor addresses/layouts, parameters and
private scratch addresses are checked; mismatch executes the skipped prefix
normally and invalidates the cached segment. External BF16 rounding is also
captured and replayed. Resident expert leases remain backend-owned.

One matched 174-token A/B pair measured 32.81 tok/s enabled versus 28.15
disabled, with byte-identical reference text. The enabled run built 13
segments, replayed 2,223 times and reported no invalidation. This single pair
does not replace production medians. A short 32-token enabled smoke run was
slower (27.67 tok/s), including first-capture overhead. Operator regression
actually exercises four builds, four replays and three invalidations through
changed integer/float parameters and interleaved prefill scratch growth, with exact BF16
reference output. Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-decode-segments-{full,full-off}.log`,
`build_cuda/decode-segments-regression-tests.log`. Additional repeated and
multi-request validation is required before enabling this by default.

Normal segment replay now compares the stored signature in place instead of
constructing per-operator temporary vectors; all address/layout/parameter
checks are retained. Three independent processes measured decode
32.28/31.63/31.78 tok/s (median 31.78), prefill 69.12/67.53/58.63 tok/s
(median 67.53), and TTFT 347.20/355.40/409.31 ms (median 355.40).
All generated the same 174-token EOS response as the earlier reference, at
about 68.44 GiB peak RSS. This validates the experimental replay configuration,
not an additional measured speedup from the allocation cleanup alone.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-segments-noalloc-{1,2,3}.log`.

An additional opt-in resident allocator experiment is enabled with
`MOLLM_RESIDENT_EXPERT_ARENA=1` (unset or `0` retains individual allocations).
It reads expert payloads directly into 64-byte-aligned slices of one anonymous
2-MiB-aligned arena, advises `MADV_HUGEPAGE`, and locks the entire arena before
slicing. Slices share ownership of the arena; active leases still prevent
teardown. There is no second expert copy or system-wide huge-page setting.
Large pages are a kernel preference, not a correctness requirement, and a
failed allocation or lock rejects resident loading rather than silently
running unlocked.

With experimental decode segments enabled, three fresh processes measured
decode 33.83/34.99/36.06 tok/s (median 34.99), prefill
71.54/71.09/70.07 tok/s (median 71.09), TTFT
335.48/337.61/342.49 ms (median 337.61), and peak RSS
70,070.8–70,081.8 MiB. All three produced the byte-identical 174-token EOS
reference response. A live second-process snapshot reported
`AnonHugePages: 66637824 kB` (63.55 GiB) and `Locked: 66723840 kB`;
this confirms actual huge-page backing, not merely an accepted advice call.
The median is 10.1% above the earlier 31.78 tok/s segment-replay median, but
these sequential batches alone do not establish a controlled causal speedup.
A subsequent fresh-process control with `MOLLM_RESIDENT_EXPERT_ARENA=0`
measured 32.01 decode tok/s, 66.22 prefill tok/s and 362.45 ms TTFT,
with the same output and 70,081.8 MiB peak RSS. This remains consistent with
an arena benefit (the arena median is 9.3% higher), but one trailing control
does not replace an interleaved repeated comparison. Log:
`build_cuda/qwen38-resident-arena-off-control.log`.
Two subsequent interleaved on/off pairs measured 34.73/30.91 and
35.61/31.56 decode tok/s (all with the same 174-token EOS text), consistent
with the earlier result. Two-sample medians are 35.17/31.235 tok/s (+12.6%);
this is repeated directional evidence, not a confidence interval or a claim
that the gain generalizes to all prompts. Peak RSS was 70,081.3–70,082.5 MiB.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-arena-interleaved-{on,off}-1.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-arena-interleaved-state{1,0}-2.log`.

A software-pipelined NVFP4 kernel that loads the next packed-weight/scale/
activation packet ahead of the current dot product was also tested and
rejected. It preserved accumulation order, but the pair-layout gate projection
changed from 121.976 to 125.285 microseconds while down changed from 65.165 to
62.253 microseconds; row-layout results also moved in opposing directions.
These microbenchmarks do not demonstrate a stable combined gain, so the
prototype was removed. Tests additionally cover `K=16` (partially active
warp) and the actual `K=640` down width. Logs:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-pipeline-{baseline,prototype}.log` and
`build_cuda/arena-interleaved-regression.log`.

The experimental segment build now exports
`CUDA_API_PER_THREAD_DEFAULT_STREAM=1` to C++ consumers in addition to nvcc's
`--default-stream=per-thread`. This keeps implicit-stream copies, memset and
benchmark events consistent with kernel launches; generated C++ and CUDA
compile flags were checked. It is a stream-semantics consistency fix, not a
claimed speedup. Five arena-enabled regression tests passed after rebuilding.
Post-fix projection timings remain comparable (pair-layout gate/down
118.671/65.047 microseconds); earlier mixed-default-stream microbenchmarks are
diagnostics, not definitive evidence for promoting a kernel change.
Logs: `build_cuda/ptds-consistency-{build,tests,projections}.log`.
The rebuilt full-model arena smoke produced the identical 174-token EOS text,
with 34.54 decode tok/s, 70.40 prefill tok/s, 340.91 ms TTFT and 70,081.1 MiB
peak RSS; segment counters were 13 builds, 2,223 replays and zero invalidations.
Log: `build_cuda/qwen38-ptds-consistency-arena.log`.

### Updated arena + segment GPU profile

A fresh node-traced Nsight Systems run of the opt-in arena/segment build
generated 32 tokens with 13 segment builds, 377 replays and zero invalidations.
Profiling throughput (32.81 tok/s) is not an uninstrumented performance result.
After excluding prefill and the first M=1 warm-up, 57,482 kernel invocations
totaled 883.34 ms within a 908.71 ms GPU timeline span. This interval includes
initial segment capture and 30 LM-head invocations. The remaining gaps are
only about 2.8% of this span; summed kernel durations must not be added to
blocking API timings, which include waits for the same GPU work.

| GPU kernel category | Time in sampled interval | Fraction |
|---|---:|---:|
| W4 dense projections | 462.35 ms | 52.3% |
| NVFP4 expert projections | 225.67 ms | 25.5% |
| W8 LM head | 77.51 ms | 8.8% |
| Other operators | 117.82 ms | 13.3% |

The broader post-prefill interval measured wide QKV W4 projections at
157.39/127.65 microseconds (N=16480/13312, K=2560), expert gate/up and down
at 97.82/58.95 microseconds, and the W8 LM head at 2592.83 microseconds.
The dense kernels remain the first optimization target; CPU launch reduction
alone has limited remaining headroom in this configuration. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-arena-segments-profile.{nsys-rep,sqlite,log}` and the
reproducible query/results `build_cuda/qwen38-arena-segments-summary.{sql,log}`.

A two-row-per-CTA prototype retained each row's original 256-thread dot and
reduction tree but did not improve N=2560/K=6144: baseline 55.689,
paired CTA 55.775, and paired CTA with shared activation caching 59.187
microseconds. Both prototypes were removed; no numerical tradeoff was
promoted. Logs: `build_cuda/q4-paired-cta-{baseline,prototype}.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-paired-cta-cache-prototype.log`, and
`build_cuda/q4-paired-cta-revert-tests.log`.

### W4 decode instruction experiments

A 192-thread (six-warp) wide projection variant retained each row's original
partial sums and reduction tree. Three paired microbenchmarks measured
N=16480/K=2560 medians 147.983 microseconds (128 threads) and 145.189
microseconds (192 threads); N=13312 showed no benefit (114.110 versus
114.234 microseconds). Restricting it to the wider cached-activation shape
still failed to improve the full model: 35.61 versus the subsequent
128-thread control's 35.69 decode tok/s, with identical output. The prototype
and its temporary `MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_WIDE_WARPS` switch were removed.
Logs: `build_cuda/q4-wide-{4,6}-paired-{1,2,3}.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-wide6-exact-tests.log`, `build_cuda/qwen38-wide6-arena.log`, and
`build_cuda/qwen38-wide4-arena-control.log`.

The biased INT4 nibble conversion now constructs the exact FP32 value using
`float_bits(0x4b400000 | (code & 15)) - 12582920.0f`. At this exponent the
mantissa increment is exactly 1.0f, producing precisely `nibble - 8` for all
16 codes. It changes neither scales nor accumulation/reduction order and
allocates no extra weight storage. Generated SASS uses mantissa construction
and an FP32 subtraction instead of converting each signed integer nibble.
The CUDA test's 18,439-row ragged wide projection still matches the original
eight-lane FP32 tree exactly, and all five targeted arena-enabled regression
tests pass, including prefill, PLE and expert-provider checks.

Three new microbenchmarks measured N=16480/K=2560 at
143.563/144.100/145.096 microseconds (median 144.100, 2.6% below the earlier
147.983-microsecond paired baseline); N=13312 measured
112.346/115.100/114.234 microseconds (median 114.234, no established gain).
This kernel measurement alone does not prove an end-to-end throughput gain.
Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-magic-nibble-prototype{,-2,-3}.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-magic-nibble-tests.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-magic-nibble-regression.log`, and
`build_cuda/q4-magic-nibble.sass`.
Three rebuilt full-model processes generated the byte-identical 174-token EOS
reference text at 36.49/35.79/33.18 decode tok/s (median 35.79),
66.30/70.07/71.03 prefill tok/s (median 70.07), and
361.99/342.52/337.91 ms TTFT (median 342.52). Peak RSS remained
70,080.8–70,081.3 MiB. Relative to the preceding 35.69-tok/s control, this
does not establish an end-to-end speedup; the noticeably slower third run
must not be discarded. The exact nibble conversion is retained on the basis
of reduced conversion work and repeatable wide-kernel improvement, without
promoting a new runtime tuning switch or claiming whole-model acceleration.
Logs: `build_cuda/qwen38-magic-nibble-arena{,-2,-3}.log`.
Arena-enabled and disabled cache tests pass, including alignment, payload,
lease-protected teardown and zero post-startup I/O; CPU cache tests and the
arena-enabled PLE/provider/tiny-model integration tests also pass.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-resident-arena.log`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-resident-arena-{2,3}.log`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-resident-arena-smaps.log`,
`build_cuda/resident-arena-final-cache-tests.log`,
`build_cuda/resident-arena-disabled-cache-tests.log`,
`build_i8mm/resident-arena-cache-tests.log`, and
`build_cuda/resident-arena-e2e-tests.log`.

A single-process interactive check additionally covers incremental follow-up,
two resets, multi-chunk prefill and translation. It correctly answered 391 and
513, completed the 421-token long response at 32.4 decode tok/s, and the
217-token translation at 32.8 tok/s, without errors. It recorded 39 segment
builds, 8,606 replays and 26 invalidations. These varied requests are correctness
smokes, not matched speed comparisons. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-segments-multiturn-input.txt`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-segments-multiturn.log`, and
`build_cuda/decode-segments-noalloc-regression-tests.log`.
An optimized translation smoke test reached EOS after 217 generated tokens
at 29.17 decode tok/s and produced the correct English translation
(`build_cuda/qwen38-optimized-translation.log`, 27 input tokens).
A separate multi-chunk prompt (136 input tokens, summary plus `19 × 27`)
reached EOS after 421 generated tokens, correctly answered `513`, and measured
91.62 prefill / 29.55 decode tok/s (`build_cuda/qwen38-optimized-long.log`).
It uses a different prompt from the earlier 120-token smoke check and is not
a matched speedup comparison.
The updated node-level Nsight trace (`qwen38-optimized-nodes-profile`) identifies
W4 dense GEMV and NVFP4 expert GEMV as the remaining dominant decode costs.
Use `--cuda-graph-trace=node` when profiling this build; graph-level tracing
does not expose the kernels inside replayed MoE subgraphs.

### Native NVFP4 Tensor Core probe and allocation-path diagnostic

A separate exact W4 packet-swizzle experiment removed two per-group lane
exchanges without changing scale or FP32 reduction order. Three 512-launch
warmup probes measured N=16480/K=2560 at 134.709/134.774/134.680 us; trailing
canonical controls measured 135.944/135.788/138.453 us. N=13312 swizzled
107.156/107.318/107.712 us versus trailing controls
107.906/108.437/108.312 us. Varied packed nibbles and non-dyadic activations
and scales match bit-for-bit, including activation offsets 1/2/3 floats.
The original wide decode exact-tree test is supplemented by a two-row
prefill test with ragged output rows and destroyed CPU weight backing.

The temporary model integration passed five targeted regressions and
generated the byte-identical 174-token EOS answer. However, its first decode
run was 34.37 tok/s; an interleaved off/on/off sequence measured
36.79/36.24/35.81 tok/s (prefill 70.12/68.82/72.79 tok/s). This does not prove
an end-to-end improvement. The production weight-layout enum, prefill
decoder branch and `MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_SWIZZLE` switch were removed; the standalone
benchmark kernels remain for layout diagnostics. A BF16 shared-activation
cache probe did not show a stable improvement and was also removed.
Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-swizzle-warm-{1,2,3}.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-cache-bf16-prototype.log`,
`build_cuda/q4-swizzle-regression.log`,
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-swizzle.log`, and
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-swizzle-interleaved-{1-state0,2-state1,3-state0}.log`.

`bench_cuda_nvfp4_mma` is an experimental standalone CUDA >=12.8 target, not
an inference backend. On the local `121a` build its generated SASS contains
`OMMA.SF.16864.F32.E2M1.E2M1.UE4M3.4X`. This establishes native NVFP4 MMA
execution on GB10; the production MoE path still decodes FP4 and accumulates
with FP32 SIMT instructions.

The probe independently checks original row/pair and MMA-repacked layouts
against CPU double accumulation over explicitly decoded W4/A4. It covers zero
activations, nonzero ragged rows (3/7/19), K=64/128/640/2560, 1/2/4/8 warps and
1/2/4/8 split-K parts, including empty splits and padded rows. Model-sized
projections use ten experts and a rotating >=128-MiB weight working set.
All variants must satisfy normalized maximum error <=2e-5 and finite outputs.
The observed synthetic activation-quantization projection relative L2 error
is approximately 6%; this is not a model PPL/accuracy validation.

Activation quantization and weight packing/copies occur outside timing;
split-K combining is included. The probe retains two representations only to
compare layouts, not as a proposed production memory design. Native decode
MMA duplicates one activation across eight columns; current coherent-host
results are approximately tied with SIMT, not an established speedup.

`MOLLM_NVFP4_PROBE_DEVICE_POOL=1|managed|pinned` isolates the allocation path
using identical weights and arithmetic. Two CUDA-device allocation runs
measured pair-layout SIMT gate/up at 83.839/84.423 us and down at
46.505/46.522 us, versus 115.702/60.016 us for the host arena run. Managed
allocation, including explicit GPU prefetch, did not reproduce this gain.
CUDA mapped pinned-host allocation measured 91.700/48.618 us in the first
pair-layout SIMT run. These are standalone memory-path diagnostics, not
full-model speed claims or proof of a specific page-table/cache mechanism.

Evidence: `build_cuda/nvfp4-native-mma-probe.sass`,
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-mma-host-diagnostic.log`,
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-mma-cuda-diagnostic{,-2}.log`,
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-mma-managed{,-prefetch}-diagnostic.log`, and
`build_cuda/nvfp4-native-mma-pinned-diagnostic.log`.
The final probe also verifies SIMT output against the separate original-FP32
activation CPU reference before timing. All four allocation modes pass both
this check and the quantized-MMA checks:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-probe-final-{0,1,managed,pinned}.log`.
The default backend remains unchanged while native activation quantization
awaits full-model precision validation.

The original checkpoint adds an important precision constraint: its
`config.json` declares static four-bit, group-16 float input quantization for
all 48 layers' experts, and the safetensors contain per-projection scalar
`input_scale`. Layer 0 / expert 0 has gate/up scales 0.0013892765 and down
scale 0.0031854538. `aggregate_nvfp4_experts` currently exports weight block
scales and per-row weight globals only, not these input scales. The current
production path uses floating activations, while the standalone MMA probe
uses synthetic dynamic-amax A4 quantization. Neither should be described
as an implementation of the checkpoint's calibrated static A4 policy.
Native-MMA integration must preserve and validate that policy rather than
silently replacing it with the probe's quantizer. No original checkpoint or
converted package was modified during this inspection.

A temporary single-copy CUDA-pinned resident arena was also tested against
the complete model. Despite the small-working-set improvement above, its two
fresh processes decoded at 23.79/23.53 tok/s and loaded in 57.85/59.61 s.
The interleaved original large-page arena control decoded at 35.40 tok/s and
loaded in 34.71 s. All generated the byte-identical 174-token EOS answer, with
13 segment builds, 2,223 hits and zero invalidations. Peak RSS remained about
70,081 MiB, so the regression was not caused by retaining a second expert copy.
The CUDA-pinned production allocator and its runtime option were removed;
only the standalone allocation-path diagnostic remains. This falsifies
extrapolating the pinned microbenchmark gain to the full 63.63-GiB expert pool,
but does not isolate the exact translation/cache mechanism.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-cuda-pinned-arena{,-2}.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-pinned-largepage-control.log`.
After removing that allocator and rebuilding, all five targeted cache,
CUDA backend, provider, PLE-offload and tiny-model integration tests pass:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-probe-final-regression.log`.

### GB10 single-payload allocation follow-up

Instruction-level sampling of the cached wide W4 kernel attributes 10,390
long-scoreboard samples to the first shuffle consuming a packed-weight load,
versus 854 and 606 at later such shuffles. The SASS already pipelines four
groups. This supports investigating weight-load readiness, not eliminating
shared activation reads. Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-wide-pc-sampling-sass.log`.

An L2-prefetch diagnostic, four groups ahead, preserves FP32 accumulation
order and compares bit-exactly. N16480/K2560 measured
116.478/117.312/115.345 us versus trailing automatic-policy controls
138.862/139.282/137.632 us. N13312/K2560 measured 92.341 versus 109.679 us.
Distances 8 and 16 were less profitable. `MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_PREFETCH=1` enables
the experimental distance-4 variant only for cached, aligned wide K2560
decode projections; it is off by default, does not change weight layout,
and does not add a weight copy. The ragged N18439 CUDA parity test passes
with it enabled. Full-model measurements are required before promoting it.
Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-l2-prefetch-{1,2,3}.log` and
`build_cuda/q4-l2-prefetch-13312.log`.

Four fresh full-model processes, alternated off/on/off/on with no concurrent
GPU workload, measured decode 32.21/37.62/34.90/36.24 tok/s and prefill
72.23/72.00/71.60/69.78 tok/s. All four generated the reference's byte-identical
174-token EOS answer. Peak RSS stayed about 70,081 MiB. Both enabled decode
runs exceeded both controls in this sequence, but the broad run-to-run
variation and only two samples per setting prevent a stable percentage
speedup claim. The option stays experimental and off by default pending
more controlled full-model repetitions. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-{1-0,2-1,3-0,4-1}.log`.

A 30-step node trace with prefetch enabled records the same 57,482 kernels
as the host control. Wide N16480/K2560 averages 120.32 us versus 146.27 us
in the control; N13312/K2560 averages 97.88 versus 116.58 us. Expert total
remains nearly unchanged (223.14 versus 222.29 ms). W4 total decreases from
433.08 to 381.81 ms, and GPU total from 837.69 to 783.80 ms. These single
traces corroborate the targeted kernel effect but are not controlled repeated
wall-clock throughput measurements; clocks are not fixed. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-summary.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-host-arena-matched-summary.log`.
CTest now also runs the backend suite in a separate process with prefetch
enabled (`test_cuda_backend_q4_prefetch`), including the ragged N18439/K2560
case, so the opt-in path does not depend on a manual environment override.

The full alternating ten-process sequence is now complete (five per setting).
Off decode samples are 32.21/34.90/35.73/36.02/36.22 tok/s, median 35.73;
on samples are 37.62/36.24/34.48/37.45/37.39, median 37.39 (+4.65%). All ten
outputs compare byte-for-byte with the reference and reach the same 174-token
EOS answer. However, prefill medians are 72.23 off and 69.91 on (-3.21%),
and the decode ranges overlap. Prefetch remains opt-in while investigating
the prefill difference and broad process-to-process variation. These medians
describe this fixed prompt/configuration, not all workloads or GPU architectures.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-1-0.log` through
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-10-1.log`, with alternating setting suffixes.

Inspecting the corresponding prefill traces narrows the interpretation of
the prefill difference: both traces contain zero wide Q4 GEMV invocations
before the first LM-head kernel. For this 24-token prompt, dense projections
use the multi-row preparation/GEMM path; `run_matmul_device` selects Q4 GEMV
only at M=1. Thus the measured cold-prefill difference is not a direct
slowdown of the prefetch kernel in this phase. This does not isolate the
source of run-to-run variation, nor generalize to single-token prefill or
ragged chunk tails. A separate warmup-1 alternating experiment follows.

That four-process warmup-1 sequence is complete. Off/on/off/on decode is
35.90/36.92/35.58/37.61 tok/s; prefill is
124.11/123.63/122.75/122.43 tok/s. All four outputs remain byte-identical.
The large cold-prefill gap does not reproduce at this size after warmup;
the two paired prefill differences are -0.39% and -0.26%. This is additional
evidence for the targeted decode optimization, not a comprehensive latency
or precision evaluation. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-warm-{1-0,2-1,3-0,4-1}.log`.

After these validations, distance-4 W4 prefetch is now the default only on
SM121 for the existing cached/aligned wide K2560 selector. Other architectures
and projection shapes keep their previous dispatch. Set
`MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_PREFETCH=0` to restore the baseline or `=1` to force the tested
prefetch selector; the override is read once per process. Automatic device
selection caches capability per thread/current GPU, avoiding a first-GPU
capability decision being reused after a device switch. The preceding
opt-in/default-off descriptions document earlier experimental stages.
CTest covers default, forced-on and forced-off dispatch in separate processes.
Standalone projection comparisons should now set `MOLLM_CUDA_Q4_PREFETCH=0`
when an unprefetched control is intended.

NVFP4 expert prefetch is a separate diagnostic, not a default optimization.
`MOLLM_NVFP4_PROBE_PREFETCH=1` checks variants one/two/four warp iterations
ahead against the original kernel, with varied packed weights/scales and both
row/pair layouts. All rotating sets are bit-exact. In the single 63.63-GiB
host expert pool, improvements are generally around noise level and do not
justify a production selector. Evidence:
`build_cuda/nvfp4-prefetch-varied-sets.log` and
`build_cuda/nvfp4-prefetch-large-host.log`.

The automatic SM121 W4 selector has now completed a full warmup-1 model run
without an environment override: 122.51 prefill / 37.55 decode tok/s,
reference-identical 174-token EOS output, RSS 70,081.7 MiB. Evidence:
`build_cuda/qwen38-q4-prefetch-default-sm121.log`.

`MOLLM_CUDA_REGISTER_ROUTES=1` is a new opt-in routing experiment. It
unrolls fixed candidate slots and invalidates the selected score with
constant-index assignments rather than a dynamic array store. The original
top-k reduction, lowest-ID tie-break, score transform, normalization and
ascending-ID output ordering remain unchanged. A 16-slot specialization
covers up to 512 experts; 32 slots cover the existing 1024-expert limit.
The compiled baseline has a 128-byte thread stack; both experimental variants
have zero stack (47 registers for 512 experts, 79 for 1024). CUDA routing
regression tests covering 1/7/33/512/1024 experts and all score functions pass
with the option enabled. Full-model timing/output validation is pending.
Evidence: `build_cuda/register-routes-resources.log`.

Explicit K-group loop unrolling at factors 2/4/8 was tested bit-exactly.
An initial factor-1 control accidentally disabled the compiler's normal
unrolling and made factor 4 look 7--9% faster. Against the restored automatic
compiler policy, N16480/K2560 factor 4 speedups were 1.001/0.976/1.001;
factors 2 and 8 were consistently slower. The experimental templates and
launchers were removed, and the original no-pragma production loop restored.
This is not a measured optimization. Evidence:
`build_cuda/q4-unroll-auto-{1,2,3}.log`; the earlier
`build_cuda/q4-unroll-16480-{1,2,3}.log` use the invalid baseline for comparing
against production and must not be cited as a speedup.

A fresh host-arena node trace using the same 30-step SQL window reports
837.69 ms GPU work over an 862.56 ms span (57,482 kernels): W4 433.08 ms,
experts 222.29 ms, head 75.40 ms, other 106.91 ms. Compared with the device
trace above, expert total differs by only 1.5%; gate/up is faster on the host
in these traces, while down is faster on device. Thus these single traces
do not support a uniform expert-allocation speedup. Clock variability remains
uncontrolled. Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-host-arena-matched-summary.log`.

Nsight Compute for N16480/K2560's existing cached wide W4 kernel shows
69.21% achieved occupancy, 75% theoretical occupancy (shared-memory limit),
85.90% scheduler cycles without an eligible warp, and approximately 93.2%
of warp waiting attributed to L1TEX long-scoreboard dependencies. Reported
compute/cache throughput is below those metrics' respective peaks. This does not
establish external-memory utilization: the restored metric audit above does
not expose the standard DRAM throughput counter. These are profiler measurements,
not end-to-end throughput predictions; the profiler's local speedup estimates
are not measured gains. Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-wide-current-details.log`.

Removing the shared activation cache in an otherwise identical wide-row
diagnostic is bit-exact but slower in three runs: 156.744/157.622/159.135 us,
versus cached controls 141.429/140.406/142.329 us. Default dispatch is unchanged.
This rules out increasing occupancy by simply dropping activation caching;
investigate weight/scale load dependencies and layout next.
Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-uncached-wide-{1,2,3}.log`. The projection benchmark
accepts optional `rows inner` arguments to isolate a shape for profiling.

A narrow W4 diagnostic preserves the exact 256-thread accumulation and
cross-warp reduction tree but removes the generic helper's two terminal
barriers. All rotating weight sets compare bit-for-bit against the original
kernel. Three runs at N2560/K6144 measured speedups of 0.943/0.933/1.032;
N320/K10240 measured 1.102/0.997/1.182. These results do not justify replacing
the production kernel, especially for the expensive N2560 shape. The variant
remains standalone diagnostic code only; default dispatch is unchanged.
Evidence: `build_cuda/q4-terminal-reduction-{1,2,3}.log`.

The NVFP4 probe can now allocate the complete 48-layer / 512-expert footprint
with `MOLLM_NVFP4_PROBE_LARGE_POOL=1`. It uses one 68,325,212,160-byte
payload, rotating layers and ten-expert selections, not two full expert copies.
These are synthetic constant weights, not a model accuracy benchmark.
With host storage, three SIMT gate timings were 118.633/118.058/118.461 us;
with `MOLLM_NVFP4_PROBE_DEVICE_POOL=1`, they were
98.733/98.150/97.941 us. Down projection improved much less, from roughly
61.4 to 58.9 us. Raw native FP4 MMA did not beat SIMT at this working-set size.
Evidence: `build_cuda/nvfp4-large-{host,cuda}-pool.log`.

The experimental production `cuda-device` resident arena passed the five
targeted regression tests, and its first full-model output is byte-identical
to the host-arena baseline. Its first decode result was 35.54 tok/s; this
does not establish an end-to-end improvement. The node-level trace records
813.44 ms of GPU work over 30 steady decode steps: W4 dense projections
414.50 ms, expert projections 218.97 ms, W8 head 79.10 ms, and other kernels
100.88 ms. Comparisons with older traces are not allocation-only experiments:
compiler/kernel changes and clocks can affect them. A matched fresh host
trace is needed before attributing changes to storage.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-cuda-device-arena.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-cuda-device-arena-summary.log`.

A subsequent isolated device run measured 36.51 decode / 69.89 prefill
tok/s, followed by a host-arena control at 36.31 / 71.18 tok/s. Both outputs
match the reference byte-for-byte. The 0.55% decode difference is too small
for a speedup claim without repeated controlled measurements. The preceding
host run in this sequence overlapped regression work and is excluded.
Evidence: `build_cuda/qwen38-arena-compare-2-device.log` and
`build_cuda/qwen38-arena-compare-3-host.log`.

## CPU

### Linux x86_64 runtime ISA dispatch

The x86 provider selects separately compiled scalar, AVX2, or AVX-512 kernels
after runtime CPUID probing. `MOLLM_X86_ISA=scalar|avx2|avx512|auto` caps the
selected tier; `MOLLM_X86_DISABLE_AVX2=1` remains a compatible scalar override.
This keeps AVX instructions out of the baseline object code and allows all
three paths to be tested from one binary.

The table below uses an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, eight threads, `M=1`, `K=2048`,
`N=6144`, five warmups, 30 measured iterations, and average throughput.

| Weight format | Scalar | AVX2 | AVX-512 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FP32 | 34.5 GFLOP/s | **43.5 GFLOP/s** | 41.5 GFLOP/s |
| FP16 | 4.3 GFLOP/s | **374.3 GFLOP/s** | 337.7 GFLOP/s |
| W8G32 | 14.4 GFLOP/s | 265.7 GFLOP/s | **338.8 GFLOP/s** |
| W4G32 | 13.7 GFLOP/s | 227.7 GFLOP/s | **265.6 GFLOP/s** |
| W4G128 | 14.4 GFLOP/s | 272.7 GFLOP/s | **436.0 GFLOP/s** |

Quantized M>1 kernels reuse each unpacked weight vector across four activation
rows. At `M=32` and 16 threads this reaches 585.0/823.3 GFLOP/s for AVX2
W4G32/W4G128 and 704.4/1091.8 GFLOP/s for AVX-512.

A Qwen3.5-0.8B W4G32 `pp256 + tg64` run at 16 threads reaches
195.52/82.26 tok/s with AVX2 and 203.28/88.19 tok/s with AVX-512. A separate
greedy generation check produced byte-identical text across scalar, AVX2, and
AVX-512. These are development measurements rather than a cross-runtime
comparison.

### Apple Silicon

The results below compare mollm with llama.cpp on an Apple M5 Pro using four
CPU threads. Unless a row says otherwise, the protocol is `pp256 + tg64`,
`warmup=3`, five independent processes, and the median throughput. `pp` is
prompt/prefill tokens per second; `tg` is generated/decode tokens per second.

## W4

All four dense/recurrent rows were refreshed on 2026-07-26 with current
packages and binaries. The dense transformer rows use BG128, with one A8 scale
per 128-value group. RWKV7 instead uses mixed W4G32: its large matrices use
32-value groups, while the vocabulary projection and small low-rank attention
adapters remain W8. Qwen3.5-4B uses a package generated by the current
converter, including fused gate/up, QKV, and linear-attention input
projections.

| Model | mollm W4 pp/tg | llama.cpp Q4_0 pp/tg | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Qwen3.5-0.8B | **868.62** / **290.54** | 797.85 / 186.52 | mollm 1.09x prefill, 1.56x decode |

## Metal

Metal support is experimental. The current optimized path covers resident
FP16, W8, and W4 packages. Results below use the same Apple M5 Pro, four CPU
threads, `warmup=3`, independent processes, and median throughput. The
matrix was refreshed on 2026-07-31.

For mollm, `--prompt-tokens 256 --max-new-tokens 65` produces one 256-token
prefill pass and exactly 64 timed decode tokens. For llama.cpp, prefill and
decode are separate processes: `-p 256 -n 0` and `-p 0 -n 64 -d 256`. The latter matters:
it measures tg64 with an existing 256-token context rather than the faster
empty-context decode path. Both runtimes keep model weights on Metal.
